content:
1	Why is this medication prescribed?
     2	 Metformin is used alone or with other medications, including insulin, to treat type 2 diabetes
     3	(condition in which the body does not use insulin normally and, therefore, cannot control the amount
     4	of sugar in the blood). Metformin is in a class of drugs called biguanides. Metformin helps to
     5	control the amount of glucose (sugar) in your blood. It decreases the amount of glucose you absorb
     6	from your food and the amount of glucose made by your liver. Metformin also increases your body's
     7	response to insulin, a natural substance that controls the amount of glucose in the blood. Metformin
     8	is not used to treat type 1 diabetes (condition in which the body does not produce insulin and
     9	therefore cannot control the amount of sugar in the blood).
    10	
    11	
    12	 Over time, people who have diabetes and high blood sugar can develop serious or life-threatening
    13	complications, including heart disease, stroke, kidney problems, nerve damage, and eye problems.
    14	Taking medication(s), making lifestyle changes (e.g., diet, exercise, quitting smoking), and
    15	regularly checking your blood sugar may help to manage your diabetes and improve your health. This
    16	therapy may also decrease your chances of having a heart attack, stroke, or other diabetes-related
    17	complications such as kidney failure, nerve damage (numb, cold legs or feet; decreased sexual
    18	ability in men and women), eye problems, including changes or loss of vision, or gum disease. Your
    19	doctor and other healthcare providers will talk to you about the best way to manage your diabetes.
    20	
    21	
    22	 How should this medicine be used?
    23	 Metformin comes as a tablet, an extended-release (long-acting) tablet, and a solution (liquid) to
    24	take by mouth. The solution is usually taken with meals one or two times a day. The regular tablet
    25	is usually taken with meals two or three times a day. The extended-release tablet is usually taken
    26	once daily with the evening meal. To help you remember to take metformin, take it around the same
    27	time(s) every day. Follow the directions on your prescription label carefully, and ask your doctor
    28	or pharmacist to explain any part you do not understand. Take metformin exactly as directed. Do not
    29	take more or less of it or take it more often than prescribed by your doctor.
    30	
    31	
    32	 Swallow metformin extended-release tablets whole; do not split, chew, or crush them.
    33	
    34	
    35	 Your doctor may start you on a low dose of metformin and gradually increase your dose not more
    36	often than once every 1–2 weeks. You will need to monitor your blood sugar carefully so your doctor
    37	will be able to tell how well metformin is working.
    38	
    39	
    40	 Metformin controls diabetes but does not cure it. Continue to take metformin even if you feel well.
    41	Do not stop taking metformin without talking to your doctor.
    42	
    43	
    44	 Ask your pharmacist or doctor for a copy of the manufacturer's information for the patient.
    45	
    46	
    47	 Other uses for this medicine
    48	 This medication may be prescribed for other uses; ask your doctor or pharmacist for more
    49	information.
    50	
    51	
    52	 What special precautions should I follow?
    53	 Before taking metformin,
    54	 tell your doctor and pharmacist if you are allergic to metformin, any of the ingredients of
    55	metformin liquid or tablets, or any other medications. Ask your pharmacist or check the
    56	manufacturer's patient information for a list of the ingredients.
    57	 tell your doctor and pharmacist what other prescription and nonprescription medications, vitamins,
    58	nutritional supplements, and herbal products you are taking. Your doctor may need to change the
    59	doses of your medications or monitor you carefully for side effects.
    60	 tell your doctor if you have or have ever had low levels of vitamin B12 in your body or any other
    61	medical conditions, especially those mentioned in the IMPORTANT WARNING section.
    62	 tell your doctor if you are pregnant, plan to become pregnant, or are breastfeeding. If you become
    63	pregnant while taking metformin, call your doctor.
    64	 tell your doctor if you eat less or exercise more than usual. This can affect your blood sugar.
    65	Your doctor will give you instructions if this happens.
    66	 What special dietary instructions should I follow?
    67	 Be sure to follow all exercise and dietary recommendations made by your doctor or dietitian. It is
    68	important to eat a healthful diet.
    69	
    70	
    71	 What should I do if I forget a dose?
    72	 Take the missed dose as soon as you remember it. However, if it is almost time for the next dose,
    73	skip the missed dose and continue your regular dosing schedule. Do not take a double dose to make up
    74	for a missed one.
    75	
    76	
    77	 What side effects can this medication cause?
    78	 This medication may cause changes in your blood sugar. You should know the symptoms of low and high
    79	blood sugar and what to do if you have these symptoms.
    80	 Metformin may cause side effects. Tell your doctor if any of these symptoms are severe, do not go
    81	away, go away and come back, or do not begin for some time after you begin taking metformin:
    82	 diarrhea
    83	 nausea
    84	 stomach discomfort
    85	 gas
    86	 indigestion
    87	 constipation
    88	 lack of energy or weakness
    89	 change in sense of taste
    90	 headache
    91	 Some side effects can be serious. If you experience any of these symptoms or those listed in the
    92	IMPORTANT WARNING section, call your doctor immediately or get emergency treatment:
    93	 chest pain
    94	 Metformin may cause other side effects. Call your doctor if you have any unusual problems while
    95	taking this medication.
    96	
    97	
    98	 If you experience a serious side effect, you or your doctor may send a report to the Food and Drug
    99	Administration's (FDA) MedWatch Adverse Event Reporting program online
   100	(https://www.fda.gov/Safety/MedWatch) or by phone (1-800-332-1088).

Based on the document in `doc.txt`, here is what is stated about Metformin:

**Uses:** Metformin is a medication in a class of drugs called biguanides. It is used alone or with other medications, including insulin, to treat type 2 diabetes — a condition in which the body does not use insulin normally and therefore cannot control the amount of sugar in the blood. Metformin helps control the amount of glucose (sugar) in the blood by decreasing the amount of glucose absorbed from food, decreasing the amount of glucose made by the liver, and increasing the body's response to insulin. The document notes that Metformin is not used to treat type 1 diabetes.

**Potential side effects:** Metformin may cause changes in blood sugar, and patients should know the symptoms of low and high blood sugar. Side effects to report to a doctor if they are severe, do not go away, or recur include: diarrhea, nausea, stomach discomfort, gas, indigestion, constipation, lack of energy or weakness, change in sense of taste, and headache. A serious side effect listed is chest pain, in which case one should call a doctor immediately or get emergency treatment. The document also states that Metformin may cause other side effects, and patients should call their doctor if they have any unusual problems while taking the medication.
